cards.#1: Elements is the flagship technical line and this polo sits at the top of the range. The Elements yardage print runs through the shirt, drawn from the collection Left of Field designed after a trip to Barnbougle. A hundred and five dollars is a lot for a polo, and it is still the first thing to buy from them.
cards.#2: Bass Strait is where the weather at Barnbougle comes from, and Left of Field named the plainest polo in the Elements line after it. It is black and unprinted, and the most wearable thing they make. At a hundred and five dollars it sits alongside the flagship with none of the graphics.
cards.#3: The weather jacket is where Elements earns the word technical. Windproof and water-repellent, with an insulated front panel and YKK hardware, in a sand and moss colourway that keeps it closer to outerwear than to golf. A hundred and forty-three dollars buys the piece doing the actual work in the line.
cards.#4: Left of Field say the grey contrast panel on the Bridport is drawn from the curving paths that weave between Barnbougle’s fairways, and Bridport is the town the course sits beside. Green body, panel across the front, a hundred and sixty-five dollars. It layers over the Elements polos without arguing with them.
cards.#5: Anderson is the bay Barnbougle overlooks, and the sweeping panel lines on the gilet are taken from the rolling dunes there. It is insulated, sleeveless, and the correct outer layer for a links course in wind. A hundred and seventy-five dollars for the thing you put over a polo when the strait is blowing.
cards.#6: The Dune is the Elements short, cut in sage on the roomier block that runs through everything Left of Field make. Mid-length, eighty-nine dollars, and the least demanding piece in the collection to get dressed in. The sage keeps it in the same range as the jacket and the gilet.
cards.#7: Left of Field cut this one pleated and wide through the leg in a technical cloth, which puts it further from a golf trouser than anything else in the Elements line. It is the pair most likely to get worn somewhere other than a course. A hundred dollars.
cards.#8: The Portsea is the heaviest outer layer in the SOUTH collection and the closest Left of Field come to a proper coat. Portsea sits at the tip of the Mornington Peninsula, an hour south of Melbourne, and the collection takes its names from that stretch of coast. Two hundred and five dollars.
cards.#9: Bridgewater Bay is on the ocean side of the peninsula, and the quarter-zip named for it is the quietest thing in SOUTH. Pale blue and clean enough to pass unremarked at a traditional club, which is a funny outcome for a brand founded on not fitting the pro shop. Two hundred and five dollars.
cards.#10: Royal blue with a textured face, the Sorrento takes its name from the town next to Portsea at the end of the Mornington Peninsula. Left of Field name their polos in pairs like that throughout the collection. A hundred and ten dollars.
cards.#11: The stripe polos are the most immediately recognisable thing Left of Field make, and this is the beige and white one, finished with a rugby collar. Mornington is the town the SOUTH collection takes its name from. Of the two stripes, the beige is the better.
cards.#12: The same shirt runs in blue and white, and between this and the beige the collection’s whole colour story is on the table. Sand and sea, and not much beyond that. A hundred and ten dollars for the cooler half of the pair.
cards.#13: Audley is the old village at the Hacking River crossing inside Royal National Park, which is the sort of reference nobody outside Sydney will catch. The vest is sage and padded, with the script wordmark on the left chest and nothing else on it. A hundred and seven dollars.
cards.#14: Stanwell Tops sits above the coast at the southern end of Royal National Park, where the escarpment drops to the sea. The trouser named for it is black, pleated and wide through the leg. It carries the surf and skate silhouette the brand was built on more plainly than anything else they make.
cards.#15: The Pintuck 2.0 is cut above the knee, roomy through the trunk and wider through the leg opening than a modern golf short has any business being. Cream is the cleanest of the four colourways. Ninety-nine dollars for the second version of the short that made the brand.
cards.#16: Navy is the safest of the Pintuck colourways and the one that will get worn most. Same block underneath as the cream: above the knee, roomy through the trunk, wide at the leg opening. Ninety-nine dollars, and the pair to start with if you are only buying one.
cards.#17: Slate arrived in July 2026, after the cream, navy and black, and it is the newest addition to the Pintuck 2.0 run. The short underneath is unchanged, cut above the knee and roomy through the trunk. Ninety-nine dollars.
cards.#18: The Resort is not a Pintuck, but it makes the same argument in a different fabric. Mocha, elasticated, and closer to a swim short than to anything hanging in a pro shop. A hundred dollars.
cards.#19: The Coastal Classic is Left of Field’s heavyweight tee, cut with relaxed shoulders and a small chest hit. It goes to the course, the brewery and the airport without changing register. Fifty-five dollars.
cards.#20: The bird on this one is a black cockatoo, a mark that recurs across the brand on ball markers, on headcovers and on the back of caps. The tee underneath is the Coastal Classic, with the same heavyweight body and relaxed shoulders. Fifty-five dollars.
cards.#21: Huskisson sits on the New South Wales south coast and gives the tee its name. The earlier runs were cut from US cotton with the artwork finished in Marrickville, in Sydney’s inner west. White, forty-eight dollars, and the plainest graphic they put on a tee.
cards.#22: A sprayed graphic on white puts this closest to the graffiti end of the founder’s reference points, which is where a lot of the brand comes from. Forty-one dollars makes it the cheapest garment they sell, and the one that reads least like golf clothing on its own.
cards.#23: Sydney Harbour Golf & Country Club does not exist. The crest is the Harbour Bridge with its two pylons replaced by golf bags, and the entire product description runs five words long: “The greatest course to never exist.” Ferry green, forty-five dollars, and the best thing Left of Field make.
cards.#24: The cap reads THE SOUTHERN SLAM / AUSTRALIAN OPEN 25 / ROYAL MELBOURNE, and Left of Field have no relationship with any of it. They sold it at a three-day pop-up in Fitzroy during that week, called it “an independent artistic interpretation” in their own copy, and stated plainly that it is not affiliated with any tournament or venue. Thirty-one dollars for bootleg tournament merch.
cards.#25: WWOG stands for Wide World Of Golf, and the cap carrying it is a navy cotton twill snapback. The brim is slightly shortened, which is what Left of Field mean when they describe it as their take on a classic vintage cap. Forty-five dollars.
cards.#26: The reversed L sits on the front as a large felt patch, with a small circular dot set into the crook that reads as a golf ball. Left of Field have never explained why it is backwards. Navy, thirty-one dollars.
cards.#27: Red plaid makes this the outlier in a range built almost entirely on sand, sage and navy. It is the one cap Left of Field make that will be the loudest thing you have on, so it works best with everything under it kept plain. Fifty dollars.
cards.#28: Albatross is a diptych and the most golf-specific thing Ciel Glue has made for Left of Field. It is hand-cut collage, printed on 250gsm and shipped unframed, so the framing is on you. Two panels also means it needs a wall with some room on it.
cards.#29: Birdie puts a golfer on a Portuguese clifftop, which is where Ciel Glue actually lives. The golf prints run on 250gsm and the surf prints on 300gsm, so the paper tells you which half of his practice you are buying. Eighty-eight dollars, unframed.
cards.#30: The Search comes from the surf side of Ciel Glue’s practice, inspired by his local break at Praia Del Rey. It explains the collaboration better than the golf prints do, because the brand and the artist arrived at golf from the same direction. Fifty-five dollars.
cards.#31: It Comes in Sets is a collage of all-female surfers, hand-cut from vintage magazines like everything else in his practice. It sits at the same fifty-five dollars as The Search, on the surf side of the pairing, and it is the furthest thing from a golf print in the collaboration.
cards.#32: Left of Field made this with Hiroki, the New Zealand bagmaker, in waxed canvas with suede and leather. The whole bag is designed around the Sydney Red Gum — Angophora costata — with an Angophora bark print on the divider and a flower logo embossed into the leather base. Three hundred and thirty dollars, and long gone.
cards.#33: Left of Field ran the inaugural Down Under (Par) Open in October 2024, a two-ball scramble at Shortees on Sydney’s Northern Beaches with a beer company sponsoring it. The bone cap is the merch from that day, which is also the day Ilias made his first career hole-in-one on the 16th. Thirty-five dollars, and gone.
cards.#34: This one is beige and brown, from the RNP collection. Its URL still reads wattamolla-polo, and Wattamolla is another beach inside Royal National Park, so an earlier name for the shirt survives in the link. Seventy-one dollars and sold out.
cards.#35: Garie is the beach at the end of the road through Royal National Park, and the polo named for it is forest green. It is the other half of the RNP pair. Seventy-one dollars and sold out.
cards.#36: Hook is the companion piece to Albatross and Left of Field have not restocked it. Ciel Glue’s golf prints go quickly, which has been the pattern with everything in the collaboration. Eighty-eight dollars when it was live.
cards.#37: The black cockatoo turns up all over the brand as a detail, and here it is cast as the whole product. Seven dollars fifty for a ball marker, and one of the few places the bird stands on its own.
cards.#38: Left of Field published this on 2 September 2022, which makes it one of the two oldest products in the catalogue and the place the brand started. Four dollars ninety for a script marker in dark green.
cards.#39: The towel runs tonal flowers on tan and has stayed sold out. Tonal on tan means the pattern reads as texture rather than as a graphic. Twenty dollars when it was live.

kickers.1: Elements is the flagship technical line, built after a 2024 trip to Barnbougle in Tasmania and photographed later on the same ground. Ilias wrote it up himself: “At Barnbougle, the land doesn’t host the course — it is the course. The wind becomes your caddie and your rival.”
kickers.2: SOUTH takes its names from the Victorian coast, an hour south of Melbourne. Portsea and Sorrento sit at the tip of the peninsula and Bridgewater Bay is on the ocean side. Mornington is the town the collection is named for.
kickers.3: Royal National Park is Australia’s oldest, gazetted in 1879 and running down the coast south of Sydney. Audley is the village at its river crossing and Stanwell sits at its southern edge. The polos carry what Left of Field call an RNP yardage print.
kickers.4: Left of Field call the original “our answer to everything wrong with golf shorts today” — roomy through the trunk, wider at the leg opening, cut to sit just above the knee. It became their best seller, and the 2.0 is a refit of the same idea.
kickers.5: The tees are boxy and mid-weight, closer to a skate shirt than a golf one. The early Clovelly and Huskisson runs were cut from US cotton with the artwork finished in Marrickville, in Sydney’s inner west.
kickers.6: Left of Field run at least five separate marks: a script wordmark, a chainstitched L, a reversed L patch, a flag insignia and a black cockatoo. Two of the caps below are not really about the logo at all.
kickers.7: Ciel Glue is a French collage artist based on the Portuguese coast, working entirely analogue with vintage magazines, old books and coloured paper. His organising idea is literary — to read the wave, extended into reading the green. Left of Field added the prints in January 2026.
kickers.8: Left of Field make small runs and let them go. What follows is a $330 collaboration bag and a $4.90 ball marker, made by the same eight-person operation four years apart.
